prompt.context: Our client is a supermarket in the UK. They have been the market leader for 50+ years; however in the past 3 years they have seen growth stall, and an upstart competitor has taken their market share. They are now at 30% market share with flat growth.
prompt.question: What is wrong with our client, and how do you help them fix the problem?

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost structure look like?
How fast is the competitor growing?
clarifying_info.a: The upstart competitor is growing at 6% per year

clarifying_info.q: Can you share any store-level data on product mix and shelf space?
clarifying_info.a: A simplified visual of a store aisle: 30 ft for Bread, 10 ft for Hair Gel, 20 ft for Frozen Meals, and 20 ft for Canned Tomatoes — each category has associated unit volumes, revenue, and profits

framework: Understand the competitive landscape: identify who the upstart competitor is, its market share trajectory, and what is driving its growth
Analyze product and category differences: compare product ranges, category margins, and which categories the competitor is growing in
Examine operational and strategic differentiation: store count, store locations and demographics, alternate sales channels (e.g. online), pricing strategy
Diagnose the root cause of the client's stalled growth by mapping findings back to the client's own product mix and shelf-space allocation
Quantify the improvement opportunity: model margin uplift from reallocating shelf space toward higher-margin categories
Develop actionable recommendations: shelf-space optimization, category mix shift, and demand-elasticity-aware planning

questions.prompt: Using the store aisle data (30 ft Bread, 10 ft Hair Gel, 20 ft Frozen Meals, 20 ft Canned Tomatoes), what happens to weekly profit if you shift 10 ft of shelf space from Bread to Hair Gel?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare profit-per-foot across categories. Bread occupies the most space but may have lower margins; Hair Gel occupies little space but earns higher margins. Shifting 10 ft from Bread to Hair Gel should yield higher total profit per aisle.

math.setup: Calculate the incremental weekly profit gain per aisle from reallocating 10 ft of shelf space from Bread to Hair Gel, then extrapolate to the full store network
steps: Estimate profit gain per aisle per week from the reallocation ≈ $30/week/aisle (derived from the unit volume, revenue, and profit data in the exhibit)
Multiply by average basket size: $50 average basket × assumed traffic implies $30 incremental profit/aisle/week
Multiply by 500 stores in the UK: $31,200 × 500 = $15,600,000/year (≈ $15M incremental profit)
Apply a P/E ratio of 10 to estimate enterprise value created: $15M × 10 = $150M in additional value
math.answer: Approximately $150 million in incremental enterprise value from a simple aisle-level shelf-space optimization across 500 UK stores

questions.prompt: What are the key factors the competitor likely optimized that the client has not?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify three dimensions: (1) elasticity of sales with respect to shelf space — how much volume responds to more or less space; (2) shifting consumer demand toward prepared/convenience foods; (3) competitive product offerings and category gaps relative to evolving consumer preferences.

brainstorming.prompt: What differences between our client and the upstart competitor could explain the competitor's 6% annual growth while our client is flat?

categories.name: Product & Category Mix
ideas: Competitor stocks different or more differentiated product categories
Competitor has higher weighting of high-margin categories (e.g. prepared foods, beauty/personal care)
Competitor has reduced low-margin commodity categories (e.g. staple dry goods)
Competitor responds faster to shifting consumer preferences toward convenience foods

categories.name: Store Operations & Shelf Management
ideas: Competitor uses data-driven shelf-space allocation optimized by margin and volume
Competitor applies demand elasticity models to determine optimal shelf footage per SKU

categories.name: Store Network & Locations
ideas: Competitor has been opening more stores
Competitor's stores are in faster-growing population areas or demographic segments
Competitor targets a younger or higher-income demographic that is growing

categories.name: Channels & Format
ideas: Competitor is growing through online/e-commerce channels
Competitor operates smaller convenience-format stores in higher-traffic locations
Competitor uses click-and-collect or home delivery

categories.name: Pricing & Promotions
ideas: Competitor has more effective promotional strategy
Competitor leverages loyalty data to personalize offers
Competitor's everyday pricing is more competitive on key value items

recommendation: The root cause of the client's stalled growth is suboptimal shelf-space allocation — the client has not optimized product mix for margin or for shifting consumer demand toward prepared and convenience foods

The client should conduct a full shelf-space optimization exercise using elasticity of sales to shelf space, updated consumer demand data, and competitive benchmarking, prioritizing high-margin categories such as prepared foods and personal care
risks: Reallocation may reduce volume of high-traffic staple categories (e.g. bread), potentially reducing store visit frequency
Consumer backlash if key staple products become hard to find
Execution risk in rolling out new planograms across 500 stores
Competitor may respond with further optimization, raising the bar
next_steps: Commission a category-level margin and elasticity analysis across all product lines
Pilot the revised shelf-space allocation in a representative set of stores before full rollout
Track basket size, visit frequency, and category sales post-pilot
Build an ongoing shelf-space optimization capability (process + tooling) to keep pace with evolving consumer preferences and competitive dynamics
